DNA and Genome.intro: DNA carries the genetic information that controls the characteristics of all living organisms. Understanding its structure and how it codes for proteins is fundamental to B6.

sections.title: DNA Structure
points: DNA is a double helix — two strands twisted around each other
Made of nucleotides — each contains a sugar, phosphate group and a base
Four bases: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C)
Complementary base pairs: A-T and G-C
DNA is found in the nucleus, coiled into chromosomes

sections.title: Genes and Proteins
points: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein
The sequence of bases determines the sequence of amino acids in a protein
Proteins control characteristics and cell processes
The human genome contains approximately 20,000-25,000 genes

sections.title: The Human Genome Project
sections.text: The Human Genome Project mapped all the genes in the human genome.
points: Allows identification of genes linked to diseases
Can develop new medicines targeted at genetic diseases
Ethical issues: genetic privacy, discrimination by employers/insurers

keyTerms.def: Deoxyribonucleic acid — molecule that carries genetic information
A section of DNA that codes for a specific protein
A long coiled strand of DNA found in the nucleus
The complete set of genetic material in an organism
Complementary bases joined by hydrogen bonds: A-T and G-C

examTips: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total).
A gene codes for ONE protein. Many genes make many different proteins.
Base pairing rules: A with T, G with C — always.
commonMistakes: Saying a gene is a whole chromosome — a gene is just a section of DNA on a chromosome.
Mixing up A-T and G-C base pairs.

Inheritance.intro: Inheritance is the passing of characteristics from parents to offspring through genes. Understanding dominant and recessive alleles and Punnett squares is essential for B6.

sections.title: Key Terms
points: Allele — a version of a gene (e.g. B = brown eyes, b = blue eyes)
Dominant — allele expressed even with one copy (capital letter)
Recessive — allele only expressed when two copies present (lower case)
Genotype — the alleles an organism has (e.g. Bb)
Phenotype — the visible characteristic (e.g. brown eyes)
Homozygous — two identical alleles (BB or bb)
Heterozygous — two different alleles (Bb)

sections.title: Punnett Squares
sections.text: Punnett squares predict the probability of offspring genotypes. For a Bb × Bb cross:

callout.label: Punnett Square
callout.text: Bb × Bb gives BB:Bb:bb in ratio 1:2:1. Probability of dominant phenotype = 3/4 (75%). Probability of recessive phenotype = 1/4 (25%).

sections.title: Sex Determination
points: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes — 22 autosomes + 1 sex chromosome pair
Female = XX, Male = XY
The Y chromosome carries the gene that triggers male development
50% chance of male or female offspring in each pregnancy

keyTerms.def: A version of a gene
Allele expressed in heterozygous individuals (capital letter)
Allele only expressed when homozygous (lower case)
The combination of alleles an organism has
The observable characteristics of an organism
Having two different alleles for a gene

examTips: Dominant does not mean more common — it just means expressed when one copy present.
Punnett squares give probabilities not certainties.
Always use correct notation: capital for dominant, lower case for recessive.
commonMistakes: Saying 'dominant = more common' — this is incorrect.
Forgetting that recessive characteristics need TWO copies of the allele.

Inherited Disorders.intro: Some disorders are caused by faulty alleles that are inherited. You need to know polydactyly (dominant) and cystic fibrosis (recessive).

sections.title: Polydactyly
points: Extra fingers or toes
Caused by a DOMINANT allele — only ONE copy needed
Even one affected parent with genotype Pp has 50% chance of passing it on
Not life-threatening

sections.title: Cystic Fibrosis
points: Causes thick sticky mucus in lungs and digestive system
Caused by a RECESSIVE allele — two copies needed (ff)
Carrier = Ff (one copy but unaffected)
Both parents must carry the allele for a child to be affected
25% chance of affected child if both parents are carriers (Ff × Ff)

sections.title: Embryo Screening
sections.text: Embryos can be screened for genetic disorders before implantation (in IVF) or during pregnancy.

callout.label: Ethical Issues
callout.text: Arguments for: prevents suffering, reduces care costs. Arguments against: embryos are destroyed, could lead to 'designer babies', discrimination against disabled people.

keyTerms.def: Having extra fingers or toes — caused by a dominant allele
Inherited recessive disorder causing thick mucus in lungs and gut
A person with one recessive allele who does not show the condition but can pass it on
Testing embryos for genetic disorders before implantation

examTips: Polydactyly = dominant (one copy enough). Cystic fibrosis = recessive (two copies needed).
A carrier of cystic fibrosis has genotype Ff — unaffected but can pass the allele on.
Be ready to evaluate embryo screening ethically.
commonMistakes: Saying carriers of cystic fibrosis are affected — they are NOT, they carry one allele.
Forgetting that both parents must be at least carriers for a recessive disorder to appear in children.

Variation and Evolution.intro: Variation between organisms can be genetic or environmental. Natural selection acts on genetic variation to drive evolution over many generations.

sections.title: Types of Variation
points: Genetic variation — caused by different alleles; inherited; cannot be changed by environment
Environmental variation — caused by conditions (diet, exercise, accidents)
Both — e.g. height is influenced by genes AND diet

sections.title: Natural Selection
numbered: Variation exists in a population (due to mutation)
These individuals are better adapted — more likely to survive and reproduce
They pass on their advantageous alleles to offspring
Over many generations, advantageous characteristics become more common

callout.label: Darwin's Key Idea
callout.text: Survival of the fittest — 'fittest' means best adapted to the environment, not strongest.

sections.title: Mutation
points: Random changes in DNA sequence
Mostly neutral — no effect on phenotype
Can be beneficial (new advantageous characteristic) or harmful
Rate increased by: radiation, some chemicals

keyTerms.def: Differences between individuals of the same species
Process where individuals with advantageous traits survive and reproduce more
A random change in DNA sequence
A feature that increases an organism's chance of survival in its environment

examTips: Natural selection requires: variation, selection pressure, survival and reproduction, inheritance.
Mutations are the SOURCE of new variation — they are random, not directed.
commonMistakes: Saying organisms 'try to adapt' — natural selection is random; there is no intent.
Confusing natural selection (process) with evolution (result over long time).

Selective Breeding and Genetic Engineeri.intro: Humans can influence the characteristics of plants and animals through selective breeding and genetic engineering, both of which have important ethical implications.

sections.title: Selective Breeding
sections.text: Selective breeding (artificial selection) involves choosing individuals with desirable characteristics to breed together over many generations.
points: Examples: disease-resistant crops, cows that produce more milk, dogs bred for specific traits
Process: select parents with desired traits → breed → select offspring with best traits → repeat over generations
Reduces genetic diversity — populations become more susceptible to new diseases

sections.title: Genetic Engineering
sections.text: Genetic engineering involves cutting a gene from one organism and inserting it into another.
points: Uses restriction enzymes to cut out the desired gene
Gene is inserted into target organism using a vector (often a plasmid)
Example: human insulin gene inserted into bacteria → bacteria produce human insulin (for diabetics)
GM crops — herbicide resistant, pest resistant, golden rice (contains vitamin A gene)
Ethical concerns: unknown long-term effects, biodiversity, 'playing God'

keyTerms.def: Choosing organisms with desired traits to breed — artificial selection
Transferring a gene from one organism to another
Genetically modified crop with useful characteristics added
Small circular DNA used as a vector in genetic engineering

examTips: Selective breeding reduces genetic diversity — a key disadvantage.
Genetic engineering inserts a specific gene; selective breeding selects for multiple traits simultaneously.
Be able to evaluate both methods — benefits and risks.
commonMistakes: Confusing selective breeding (natural alleles selected) with genetic engineering (gene transferred from different species).
Forgetting that selective breeding reduces genetic diversity.

Evidence for Evolution.intro: There is extensive evidence that all life on Earth evolved from a common ancestor. Understanding this evidence is important for B6.

sections.title: Fossil Evidence
points: Fossils show how organisms have changed over time
Found in sedimentary rock — older fossils deeper down
Gaps in fossil record exist because: soft tissue rarely fossilises, conditions not always right for preservation
Despite gaps, fossils show a clear progression of life forms

sections.title: Antibiotic Resistance
sections.text: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria is evolution by natural selection happening in real time:
numbered: Random mutation gives some bacteria resistance
Resistance gene becomes common in population

sections.title: Why Darwin's Theory Was Controversial
points: Challenged religious beliefs about creation
Darwin had no knowledge of genes or DNA at the time
Limited fossil evidence in Darwin's era
Theory gradually accepted as more evidence emerged

keyTerms.def: Preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms in rock
Change in inherited characteristics of a population over many generations
An ancestral species from which different species have evolved

examTips: Antibiotic resistance is EVIDENCE for evolution by natural selection — happening now.
The fossil record is incomplete but still strongly supports evolution.
commonMistakes: Saying fossils disprove evolution because there are gaps — gaps exist due to preservation conditions, not because evolution didn't happen.

Classification.intro: Classification is the grouping of organisms based on their characteristics. Modern classification uses evolutionary relationships based on DNA evidence.

sections.title: The Classification System
sections.text: The Linnaean system classifies organisms into groups:
points: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Memory aid: 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup'
Binomial nomenclature: genus + species name (e.g. Homo sapiens — always italicised or underlined)

sections.title: The Three-Domain System
sections.text: Carl Woese proposed a three-domain system based on molecular evidence:
points: Archaea — primitive bacteria (extremophiles)
Bacteria — true bacteria
Eukaryota — all organisms with a nucleus (including plants, animals, fungi)
Based on ribosomal RNA sequences — more accurate than morphology alone

sections.title: Evolutionary Trees
points: Show evolutionary relationships between organisms
Based on DNA similarity — more similar DNA = more recently shared common ancestor
Can override physical appearance — some organisms look similar but are not closely related

keyTerms.def: Grouping organisms based on shared characteristics
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
Two-part naming system using genus and species (e.g. Homo sapiens)
Classification into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota based on molecular evidence

examTips: The three-domain system is based on DNA/RNA evidence — more reliable than physical appearance.
Binomial names: first word is genus (capital), second is species (lower case) — both italicised.
Know the order: Kingdom Phylum Class Order Family Genus Species.
commonMistakes: Capitalising the species name — only the genus is capitalised in binomial nomenclature.
Forgetting that the three-domain system replaced the five-kingdom system.
